title: At the Hotel
subtitle: Booking a room by phone, and checking out when the bill has something on it you did not expect.
description: An A2 listening and reading page with two model hotel dialogues — reserving a room and checking out, including querying a charge on the bill.
passage: Two conversations at a hotel. The guest's lines are written out here as models. Read them, then cover them and try the dialogue yourself.
1. Booking a room
Receptionist: Good afternoon, the Lakeview Hotel. May I help you?
You: Good afternoon. I'd like to book a room, please.
Receptionist: Certainly. For which dates?
You: For the nights of June 3rd and 4th.
Receptionist: And how long will you be staying?
You: Two nights. I'll check out on the morning of the 5th.
Receptionist: What kind of room would you like?
You: A double room with a private bathroom, if you have one.
Receptionist: Let me check what's available… Yes, we have a room on the fourth floor with a view of the lake.
You: That sounds perfect. How much is it per night?
Receptionist: A hundred and forty dollars, including breakfast.
You: Does that include tax?
Receptionist: Tax is extra — it comes to about sixteen dollars a night.
You: All right, I'll take it. The name is Karen Jones.
Receptionist: Thank you, Ms. Jones. We'll see you on the third.
2. Checking out
Receptionist: Good morning. May I help you?
You: Good morning. I'd like to check out, please. Room 412.
Receptionist: One moment, please, ma'am… Here's your bill. Would you like to check that the amount is correct?
You: Thank you. Excuse me — what's this charge here, for eighteen dollars?
Receptionist: That's for the phone calls made from your room.
You: I see. I didn't realize the room phone was charged separately.
Receptionist: It is, I'm afraid. Would you like me to print the call log?
You: No, that's all right. And could I pay by card?
Receptionist: Certainly. May I see some ID?
You: Here's my passport.
Receptionist: Thank you. Could you sign here for me?
You: Of course. Could I also get a receipt for my company?
Receptionist: Here are your receipt and your card, ma'am. Thank you for staying with us.
You: Thank you — we had a very comfortable stay.

vocabulary.term: to check in / to check out
vocabulary.definition: to arrive and register / to pay and leave
a room with a bed for two people (compare: a single room)
an amount of money added to your bill for something
the paper showing what you owe (in restaurants, American English prefers 'the check')
money added by the government; in US hotels it is usually not in the advertised price
a polite way to introduce bad news

items.prompt: Receptionist: "How long will you be staying?"
items.explanation: 'How long' asks about duration. 'On the third' answers when you arrive.

items.prompt: You want a room for two people. You ask for:
items.explanation: A double room has a bed for two; a single is for one person.

items.prompt: You do not understand an amount on the bill. You say:
options: Excuse me — what's this charge for?
items.explanation: Asking what a charge is for is polite and gets you an answer. Accusing first does not.
The request is for a document, so hand one over.

items.prompt: You need proof of payment for your employer. You ask:
items.explanation: A receipt proves you paid; a bill shows what you owe.

items.prompt: The receptionist has to give you bad news politely. She says:
items.explanation: "I'm afraid" used this way softens bad news and is very common in service English.

items.prompt: I'd like to ___ out at ten tomorrow morning.
items.explanation: You check out when you leave a hotel.

items.prompt: What is this ___ for eighteen dollars?
items.explanation: A charge is an amount added to your bill.

items.prompt: In US hotels, ___ is usually added on top of the advertised price.
items.explanation: Hotel tax is normally extra — a common surprise for visitors.

items.prompt: Could I have a ___ for my company, please?
items.explanation: A receipt is the proof of payment you submit for expenses.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the dialogues.

items.statement: The room is on the fourth floor and looks out at the lake.
items.explanation: True — "a room on the fourth floor with a view of the lake".
False — breakfast is included, but tax is extra, about $16 a night.

items.statement: The guest is staying three nights.
items.explanation: False — two nights, the 3rd and the 4th, checking out on the 5th.

items.statement: The extra charge was for phone calls from the room.
items.explanation: True — the receptionist explains exactly that.

items.statement: The guest asks for the call log to be printed.
items.explanation: False — it is offered, but the guest says "No, that's all right".

discussion: Role-play dialogue 1: one of you is the receptionist, the other books a room for a specific weekend.
Have you ever found a charge on a bill you did not expect? What did you do?
In the US, hotel prices usually exclude tax, and restaurant prices exclude the tip. Is that the same where you live?
Write a dialogue (about 10 lines) in which you check into a hotel and ask two questions about the room.
